items.plain: I was hardly aware of myself as a separate person, but felt strongly the fire inside me, as if I were pure activity and my hands and feet were just tools my spirit was trying out.
items.core_idea: A child feels herself as spirit, the body its instrument

items.plain: At first I spent many sunny hours starting long, complicated designs, but I soon learned, by punishing myself, to avoid complex patterns, because I had to finish whatever I started.
items.core_idea: Finishing what you start teaches you to choose carefully

items.plain: I loved my aunt three times over: for her big laugh, for how she cheered my mother, and most of all for drying my tears and holding me after my mother scolded me.
items.core_idea: We love most those who comfort us

items.plain: Watching my mother disappear, I felt heavy regret and sudden weakness. Among strangers she didn't fully trust, I could no longer be myself or speak my feelings, and crying now changed nothing.
items.core_idea: Among strangers you lose the freedom to be yourself

items.plain: I had reached the wonderful place I'd dreamed of, but I wasn't happy. Exhausted, I cried myself to sleep, and my tears dried on their own because no one who loved me was there.
items.core_idea: Arriving where you hoped can still leave you lonely

items.plain: When they cut my braids, my spirit broke. Since being taken from my mother I had been stared at, tossed like a puppet and shamed; no one comforted me, and I was just one of a herd.
items.core_idea: Being stripped of dignity breaks the spirit

items.plain: The sadness of those dark days still shadows my years. However stormy it feels inside me, it comes out only as a quiet voice, heard only by those who listen with compassion.
items.core_idea: Old sorrow speaks softly, heard only by compassionate listeners

items.plain: I felt suspended in chaos, beyond anyone's help. My brother and my mother couldn't understand me, and even nature had no place for me: I was neither child nor grown, neither wild Indian nor tame one.
items.core_idea: Belonging nowhere, between two worlds, feels like chaos

items.plain: As I left the stage, my fellow students surprised me with a big bouquet of roses. Their kindness was a rebuke for the hard feelings I had held against them.
items.core_idea: Unexpected kindness shames the resentment we held

items.plain: Alone in my room after winning, I stopped laughing. That small victory didn't satisfy the hunger in my heart, and I pictured my mother far away, holding something against me.
items.core_idea: Winning cannot fill a heart estranged from home

items.plain: For a moment I laughed at my bad luck and meant to improve things, but a heavy weakness came over me, like years of tiredness, and I lay down and forgot my good intention.
items.core_idea: Deep weariness swallows good intentions

items.plain: Worn out and unable to keep any faith, I cried to my mother to stop praying, saying the Great Spirit doesn't care if we live or die, and that if we expect no justice we can't be disappointed.
items.core_idea: Despair gives up on hope to avoid disappointment

items.plain: For the white man's education I gave up the Great Spirit, nature's healing, my mother and any friends. Like a tree uprooted from mother, nature and God, I was stripped of branches and bark, raw.
items.core_idea: Trading roots for success leaves you uprooted and raw

items.plain: When my spirit is full I wander the hills or sit by the river, small as a grain of sand, feeling the loving Mystery all around me in clouds, water and summer warmth, and I quietly grow.
items.core_idea: Resting in nature, you feel the loving Mystery and grow

items.plain: Back at my desk I feel kinship with all creatures again. Racial lines once bitterly real now mark a living mosaic, and people of one color are like piano keys, alike yet each distinct.
items.core_idea: All people are kin, alike yet each distinct

items.plain: The missionary and the native believer are both God's creatures, though their idea of Infinite Love is small. I prefer nature to their dogma: there I hear the Great Spirit, and the universe is His robe.
items.core_idea: The Great Spirit is heard in nature, beyond dogma

items.plain: I sat with my parents as before but didn't feel at home. My mother and I wept together, yet our beliefs kept us far apart: I grieved for an unsaved soul, she for a brave man's broken body.
items.core_idea: Shared grief can still be divided by belief

items.plain: "Who am I?" had become the riddle of Blue-Star Woman's life. The white man's law demanded proof she belonged to her tribe, but her heart simply said: I am a being, I am Blue-Star Woman, the earth is my birthright.
items.core_idea: Identity is a birthright, not something papers prove

items.plain: He fought a terrible inner battle harder than ever before. Against all odds he clung to an ancient hope of rescue and refused to give up his faith in good people.
items.core_idea: Holding on to faith in good people against all odds

items.plain: Every skill, every field of knowledge, and every action and choice seems to aim at some good, which is why the highest good has fairly been described as what everything aims at.
items.core_idea: Everything we do aims at some good

items.plain: Nearly everyone calls the goal happiness and equates it with living well, but people disagree about what it is: pleasure, wealth, honour, or health when sick and money when poor, and they admire those who talk over their heads.
items.core_idea: Everyone wants happiness but disagrees on what it is

items.plain: Self-sufficient does not mean living alone; it includes parents, children, spouse, friends and fellow citizens, because humans are by nature made for life with others.
items.core_idea: Humans are by nature social beings

items.plain: If carpenters and cobblers each have their proper work, and the eye, hand and foot each have a function, surely a human being as such must also have some work of their own.
items.core_idea: A human being has a proper work of their own

items.plain: Happiness must take a whole life: just as one swallow or one fine day doesn't make a spring, one day or a short time doesn't make someone truly happy.
items.core_idea: One good day does not make a happy life

items.plain: At the Olympics the prize goes not to the finest and strongest but to those who compete; likewise in life, among good and honourable people, it is those who act who rightly win.
items.core_idea: Prizes go to those who act, not merely the able

items.plain: Small strokes of luck don't change a life, but great misfortunes bruise happiness, bringing pain and blocking action. Still, nobility shines through when someone bears many great misfortunes calmly, not because they feel no pain but because they are noble.
items.core_idea: Nobility shines when great misfortune is borne calmly

items.plain: A truly good and sensible person bears every fortune with grace and does the best possible in the circumstances, as a good general uses the troops he has or a shoemaker makes the finest shoe from the leather given.
items.core_idea: Make the best of whatever you are given

items.plain: In both the person who controls their appetites and the one who tries and fails, we praise reason for urging the right course, but clearly something else in us naturally fights against reason.
items.core_idea: Something in us fights against our reason

items.plain: We gain virtues by practising them, as with any craft: people become builders by building and harpists by playing, and in the same way we become just by doing just acts, self-controlled by self-control, and brave by brave acts.
items.core_idea: We become good by repeatedly doing good acts

items.plain: The test of a habit is how its acts feel afterwards: the self-controlled person is glad to give up bodily pleasures, not sorry; the brave person faces danger with pleasure or at least without pain.
items.core_idea: True virtue feels glad, not grudging

items.plain: Virtues come from doing virtuous actions, yet most people retreat into talk and think philosophising will make them good, like patients who listen closely to the doctor but do nothing he says, and stay sick.
items.core_idea: Talking about goodness without doing it changes nothing

items.plain: Virtue concerns feelings and actions, which can be too much or too little. Feeling fear, anger, pity or pleasure at the right time, about the right things, toward the right people, rightly, is the mean: virtue.
items.core_idea: Virtue is feeling rightly, neither too much nor too little

items.plain: There are countless ways to go wrong but only one way to go right, so missing the mark is easy and hitting it hard. That is why excess and deficiency belong to vice and the mean to virtue.
items.core_idea: Many ways to go wrong, only one to go right

items.plain: Being good is hard because finding the mean takes skill. Anyone can get angry or spend money, but doing it to the right person, in the right amount, at the right time and rightly is rare and noble.
items.core_idea: Anyone can get angry; doing it rightly is rare

items.plain: Notice your own natural leaning, which shows in what pleases and pains you, and push yourself the other way; you reach the middle by moving far from your error, as people straighten bent wood.
items.core_idea: Correct your bias by leaning the other way

items.plain: It is sometimes hard to decide what to choose over what, or what to endure instead of what, and harder still to stick to the decision, because the options are painful and the actions demanded are shameful.
items.core_idea: Hard choices are hard to make and harder to keep

items.plain: It is absurd to blame outside things for your actions instead of your own readiness to be caught by them, or to take credit for your good acts while blaming pleasure for the bad ones.
items.core_idea: Don't blame circumstances for your own weakness

items.plain: We deliberate about matters that follow general rules yet are uncertain in a given case, and for big matters we bring in others to advise us, not trusting ourselves to decide alone.
items.core_idea: For big decisions, seek others' counsel

items.plain: Most people are misled by pleasure: though it is not truly good, it seems good to them, so they choose the pleasant as good and avoid pain as bad.
items.core_idea: Pleasure fools us into thinking it is good

items.plain: Whoever knowingly acts in ways that make him unjust is unjust by choice, yet cannot simply wish to be just again, like a sick man who ignored his doctor. Like a thrown stone, it was once in his power.
items.core_idea: Habits chosen freely can become impossible to undo

items.plain: The brave person, as far as a human can be, is not frightened out of doing right; he will feel fear, but he faces it as he should and as reason directs, for the sake of what is honourable.
items.core_idea: Courage feels fear but faces it for the right reason

items.plain: Rash people are eager before danger but back off once in it, while brave people are calm beforehand and quick and sharp when action comes.
items.core_idea: The brave are calm before danger and sharp within it

items.plain: Dying to escape poverty, heartbreak or any pain is not brave but cowardly: it is softness to flee hardship, and such a person faces death not because it is honourable but to get away from suffering.
items.core_idea: Fleeing pain through death is not courage

items.plain: Courage involves pain and is rightly praised, because it is harder to endure what is painful than to hold back from what is pleasant.
items.core_idea: Enduring pain is harder than resisting pleasure

items.plain: Death and wounds pain the brave person, yet he endures them because it is honourable. The better his life, the more death pains him, since he loses most; feeling this makes him no less brave, perhaps more.
items.core_idea: Courage is greater when one has more to lose

items.plain: The person without self-control craves pleasures above all else, and suffers both when he misses them and in the craving itself, since all desire involves pain. Strange, to be pained because of pleasure.
items.core_idea: Craving pleasure itself brings pain

items.plain: Unless appetite obeys reason it grows huge: the fool's hunger for pleasure is endless, each indulgence strengthens the habit, and strong desires can drive out reason altogether. So desires should be moderate, few, and never against reason.
items.core_idea: Each indulgence feeds appetite until it overrules reason

items.plain: Generosity depends not on how much is given but on the giver's character, giving in proportion to what he has. So someone who gives less may be more generous, if he has less to give.
items.core_idea: Generosity is measured by means, not amount

items.plain: The generous person rarely gets rich, since he gives freely rather than taking or keeping. People blame fortune that the most deserving are least wealthy, but it is reasonable: you can't have wealth without caring to keep it.
items.core_idea: The generous seldom grow rich, and that is reasonable

items.plain: Rating yourself highly without good reason is vanity; rating yourself below your real worth is small-mindedness. The worst case is a person of great worth who undervalues himself: what would he do if he were worth less?
items.core_idea: Undervaluing real worth is as wrong as vanity

items.plain: The great-minded person handles wealth, power and every kind of good or bad fortune with moderation, however things turn out, neither overjoyed when they go well nor overly pained when they go badly.
items.core_idea: Stay even-tempered through good fortune and bad

items.plain: The small-minded person, through self-ignorance, denies himself what he deserves. He isn't foolish, just holding back, but this low self-opinion harms character: people aim by what they think they deserve, so he avoids honourable actions.
items.core_idea: Thinking yourself unworthy keeps you from worthy deeds

items.plain: Bitter-tempered people stay angry long because they bottle it up; only revenge brings relief. Otherwise the weight stays, since hidden anger can't be talked away and takes time to digest, burdening them and their closest friends.
items.core_idea: Bottled-up anger weighs on you and those close

items.plain: In social life, some people agree with everything and never object, wanting only to please and give no pain; others oppose everything and don't care at all whether they hurt anyone.
items.core_idea: Pleasing everyone and opposing everyone are both faults

items.plain: Some rest and amusement in life are generally thought to be essential.
items.core_idea: Rest and play are necessary in life

items.plain: The worst person practises vice both personally and toward his friends; the best practises virtue not only personally but toward his neighbour, which is genuinely hard.
items.core_idea: The best people practise goodness toward others too

items.plain: One unjust act doesn't by itself make an unjust person. A man who sins with another's wife from passion, not deliberate choice, acts wrongly but hasn't necessarily an unjust character; one can steal without being a thief.
items.core_idea: One wrong act does not make a wrong character

items.plain: People think acting justly is easy because the acts are easy. But doing them from the right inner disposition is hard, like medicine: knowing remedies is easy, but knowing how, to whom and when makes a doctor.
items.core_idea: Knowing what is just is easy; acting justly is hard

items.plain: Being treated unjustly and treating others unjustly are both bad, one having too little and the other too much, but doing injustice is worse, because it involves wickedness and blame, while suffering injustice does not.
items.core_idea: Doing wrong is worse than suffering wrong

items.plain: A practically wise person deliberates well about what is good for himself, not in one narrow area like health but for living well. Calculating well toward a good end where no fixed rule applies is wisdom.
items.core_idea: Practical wisdom is deliberating well about living well

items.plain: Pay attention to the unproven sayings and opinions of experienced, older and practically wise people as much as to strict arguments, because experience has given them an eye for seeing rightly.
items.core_idea: Experience gives the wise an eye for what is right

items.plain: Anger listens to reason but mishears it, like servants who rush off before hearing the whole order, or dogs barking before seeing friend or foe; hot and quick, it rushes to revenge before reason finishes.
items.core_idea: Anger rushes off before reason finishes speaking

items.plain: Stubborn people resemble the self-controlled but differ: the self-controlled person is not swayed by passion yet can be persuaded when right; the stubborn one won't change even for reason, and is often led by pleasures.
items.core_idea: Stubbornness resists reason; self-control resists passion

fix.display_text: There are also people, who have a trick of abiding by their own opinions, who are commonly called Positive, as they who are hard to be persuaded, and whose convictions are not easily changed: now these people bear some resemblance to the character of Self-Control, just as the prodigal to the liberal or the rash man to the brave, but they are different in many points. The man of Self-Control does not change by reason of passion and lust, yet when occasion so requires he will be easy of persuasion: but the Positive man changes not at the call of Reason, though many of this class take up certain desires and are led by their pleasures.

items.plain: Practice, friend, lasts a long time, and in the end it becomes your very nature.
items.core_idea: Long practice becomes second nature

items.plain: Friendship is tied to virtue and most necessary for life: no one would choose to live without friends even with every other good. The prosperous need friends, and in poverty or trouble friends are the only refuge.
items.core_idea: No one would choose life without friends

items.plain: The dry earth loves the rain, and the heavy sky, full of rain, loves to fall on the earth.
items.core_idea: Opposites long for each other

items.plain: The young are easily given to love, since it runs on impulse and pleasure; so they form friendships and drop them quickly, sometimes within a day, yet they want to spend time closely with their friends.
items.core_idea: Friendships built on pleasure come and go quickly

items.plain: Perfect friendship exists between good people alike in goodness, who wish each other well for the friend's own sake, not for what they get. Such friendship lasts as long as they stay good, and goodness tends to last.
items.core_idea: True friendship wishes good for the friend's own sake

items.plain: People who quickly start doing friendly things for each other may want to be friends, but they aren't unless each is worthy and each knows it; the wish for friendship comes fast, friendship itself does not.
items.core_idea: The wish for friendship is quick; friendship is slow

items.plain: Friendships based on profit are weaker and shorter-lived; such friends usually part when the advantage ends, because they were never friends of each other, only of the advantage.
items.core_idea: Friends for profit were only friends of the profit

items.plain: Friends who live together enjoy and help each other; friends apart stay friendly but can't act on it. Distance doesn't end friendship, but long absence can make people forget it: lack of contact destroys many friendships.
items.core_idea: Long absence lets friendships fade

items.plain: You can't have perfect friendship with many people, just as you can't be in love with many at once. It is hard to delight in many, or find many truly good, and it takes experience and intimacy.
items.core_idea: Deep friendship is possible with only a few

items.plain: Friendship lies more in loving than being loved, as mothers show: some who give their children to be raised by others keep loving them without asking anything back, content to see them well, even unloved in return.
items.core_idea: Friendship lies more in loving than being loved

items.plain: Equality and likeness bind friends, especially likeness in goodness: good people are steady in themselves and with others, never asking or doing degrading things, since the good neither do wrong nor let their friends do it.
items.core_idea: Good friends keep each other from doing wrong

items.plain: Parents love their children as part of themselves, children love parents as their source, and siblings love each other because they share one origin; hence talk of the same blood and root.
items.core_idea: Family love springs from shared origin

items.plain: Friendship between husband and wife is natural, since people are made to pair even more than to form communities. They live together not only to have children but for all of life, dividing tasks and sharing contributions.
items.core_idea: Marriage is a natural partnership for all of life

items.plain: Complaints arise mainly in friendships of usefulness. Friends in goodness are eager to be kind to each other, so there is no quarrel; no one resents being loved and helped, and both get what they seek: the good.
items.core_idea: Friends in goodness compete only in kindness

items.plain: Between unequal friends, the one who receives should repay with honour as far as he can, because friendship asks what is possible, not what is owed; no one can fully repay the gods or parents.
items.core_idea: Friendship asks what is possible, not what is owed

items.plain: If a friend turns out a scoundrel, you needn't stay friends, since only the good deserves friendship. Don't break off at once unless he is beyond repair; help mend his character. Ending it isn't wrong: he has changed.
items.core_idea: Help a friend gone wrong; leave only if incurable

items.plain: If one friend grows greatly in goodness while the other stays as he was, like boyhood friends where only one matures, they can't stay friends. Still, the one who grew should show regard for the old closeness.
items.core_idea: Outgrown friends still deserve regard for the past

items.plain: Our feelings for friends seem to grow from how we feel toward ourselves. A friend is one who does good to another for their sake, wants them to live, shares their choices, or shares their sorrows and joys.
items.core_idea: A friend wants your good for your own sake

items.plain: The good person enjoys his own company: his memories please him, his hopes are good, his mind has much to think about, and his joys and griefs stay consistent from day to day, since he has little to regret.
items.core_idea: A good person can live happily with himself

items.plain: A wicked person can't even be a friend to himself, having nothing lovable within. Since that is miserable, flee wickedness with all your strength and strive to be good, to befriend yourself and others.
items.core_idea: Become good to be a friend to yourself

items.plain: Goodwill is not yet friendship: it can arise suddenly, even toward strangers, without action or intensity. Yet it is where friendship begins, as being pleased by someone's looks begins love; with time and closeness it can ripen into real friendship.
items.core_idea: Goodwill is the seed from which friendship grows

items.plain: People love most what cost them most effort, as those who earned money love it more than heirs. Giving kindness takes effort, receiving doesn't; so mothers, who labour most, love their children most, as benefactors do.
items.core_idea: We love most what costs us effort

items.plain: The good person does much for friends and country, even dying for them. He gives up money and honours for what is noble, preferring a short intense joy to a long mild one, one noble year to many ordinary.
items.core_idea: Better one noble year than many ordinary ones

items.plain: It is absurd to picture the happy person alone: no one would choose every good on condition of solitude, since humans are social by nature. Friends and good people beat strangers, so the happy person needs friends.
items.core_idea: Even the happiest person needs friends

items.plain: Friends are more needed in hard times, and more honourable to have in good times. Their very presence is pleasant even in trouble, because grieving people are comforted by friends' sympathy.
items.core_idea: Friends' sympathy comforts us in grief

items.plain: Invite friends readily to share good fortune, but reluctantly to share bad, burdening them little. Go to friends in trouble unasked and eagerly, be slow to share in their gains, and don't sullenly refuse their help.
items.core_idea: Share joys freely; go to friends in trouble unasked

items.plain: Friendship between wicked people turns corrupt as they grow alike in bad ways. Friendship between good people grows as they spend time together, improving each other through shared acts and correction: you learn good from the good.
items.core_idea: Good friends make each other better

items.plain: There are many things we would pursue even without pleasure, such as seeing, remembering, knowing and having virtues; that pleasure naturally follows makes no difference, because we would choose them anyway.
items.core_idea: Some things are worth having even without pleasure

items.plain: No one feels pleasure all the time because we tire; our faculties can't work without pause, and pleasure follows activity. New things please at first because the mind engages fully, but later attention slackens and the pleasure dulls.
items.core_idea: Pleasure fades as attention slackens

items.plain: Happiness doesn't lie in amusement; toiling all your life for fun is absurd and childish. But amusing yourself so you can work well afterwards is right, since amusement is rest, and we can't work non-stop.
items.core_idea: Play is rest for work, not life's goal

items.plain: Don't heed those who say a mortal should think only of mortal things. As far as you can, live by the highest part of yourself, which, though small, far surpasses everything else in power and worth.
items.core_idea: Live by the highest part of yourself

items.plain: Though happiness needs some external goods, it doesn't need many or great ones; you can act nobly without ruling land and sea, since even with moderate means a person can live virtuously.
items.core_idea: Moderate means are enough to live well

items.plain: In moral matters the goal is not theory and knowledge but practice; so knowing about virtue is not enough. We must also try to have it and use it, and take whatever other means there are of becoming good.
items.core_idea: Knowing about goodness is not enough; practise it

items.plain: The saying "as a man thinks in his heart, so is he" covers a person's whole being and every circumstance of life: you literally are what you think, your character being the total of all your thoughts.
items.core_idea: You are what you think

items.plain: The mind is like a garden that grows something whether tended or not; neglected, it fills with weeds. Weed out wrong, impure thoughts and grow right, pure ones, and you find you are the master gardener of your soul.
items.core_idea: Tend your mind like a garden

items.plain: As a growing being, a person is where he is in order to learn and grow; once he learns the spiritual lesson a circumstance holds for him, it passes and gives way to other circumstances.
items.core_idea: Circumstances pass once we learn their lesson

items.plain: A person is tossed about by circumstances as long as he believes he is their creature; once he realises he is a creative power who can direct the hidden seeds circumstances grow from, he becomes master of himself.
items.core_idea: Knowing you can shape circumstances makes you their master

items.plain: People want better circumstances but won't improve themselves, so they stay stuck. Whoever doesn't shrink from sacrificing himself will reach what his heart is set on; even getting rich demands sacrifice, so how much more a strong, balanced life?
items.core_idea: To change circumstances, first be willing to change yourself

items.plain: Good thoughts and acts never bring bad results, nor bad ones good: corn yields only corn, nettles only nettles. People follow this law in nature, but few see it works just as surely in the mind and morals.
items.core_idea: Good thoughts bear good fruit, bad thoughts bad

items.plain: You begin to be a real man when you stop whining and cursing and look for the hidden justice ruling your life; then you stop blaming others, think nobly, and use circumstances to grow and find your hidden powers.
items.core_idea: Stop blaming; use circumstances to grow

items.plain: Any line of thought kept up, good or bad, will shape character and circumstances. You can't directly choose your circumstances, but you can choose your thoughts, and so shape your circumstances indirectly but surely.
items.core_idea: Choose your thoughts and you shape your circumstances

items.plain: Give up sinful thoughts and the world softens toward you; drop weak thoughts and opportunities appear; nurture good thoughts and no hard fate can keep you miserable. The world is a kaleidoscope mirroring your changing thoughts.
items.core_idea: The world mirrors your thoughts

items.plain: To protect your body, guard your mind; to renew it, beautify your mind. Malice, envy, disappointment and gloom rob the body of health and grace; sour thoughts make a sour face, and folly, passion and pride make wrinkles.
items.core_idea: Guard your mind to protect your body

items.plain: Cheerful thought heals the body like no doctor, and goodwill comforts grief like nothing else. Living in ill will, suspicion and envy is a self-made prison; thinking well of all and finding their good brings deep peace.
items.core_idea: Goodwill toward all brings peace; ill will imprisons

items.plain: Set a worthy purpose in your heart, spiritual or worldly, make it the centre of your thoughts, and don't let your mind drift into passing fancies. Even if you fail repeatedly, the strength of character gained is your true success.
items.core_idea: Fix your thoughts on one purpose; failures build strength

items.plain: Even the weakest soul, knowing its weakness and believing strength comes only through effort and practice, will start trying, and by adding effort to effort and patience to patience will keep growing until it becomes divinely strong.
items.core_idea: Strength grows through steady effort and patience

items.plain: The will to act comes from knowing we can. Doubt and fear are the great enemies of that knowledge, and whoever feeds them instead of killing them blocks himself at every step.
items.core_idea: Doubt and fear block the will to act

items.plain: A strong person can't help a weaker one unless the weaker is willing, and even then the weak must grow strong by his own effort; no one but himself can change his condition.
items.core_idea: No one but yourself can change your condition

items.plain: Small achievements need small sacrifices; great achievements need great ones; the highest attainments need the greatest sacrifice.
items.core_idea: Achievement is measured by sacrifice

items.plain: Every great achievement began as a dream. The oak sleeps in the acorn, the bird waits in the egg, and in the soul's highest vision an angel is stirring. Dreams are the seedlings of reality.
items.core_idea: Dreams are the seeds of reality

items.plain: Careless, lazy people see only results and call them luck, favour or chance. They don't see the trials, failures, sacrifices, effort and faith others went through to reach their vision, only the bright end, never the dark, hard road.
items.core_idea: What people call luck is unseen effort

items.plain: In everything there is effort and result, and the result matches the strength of the effort; there is no chance. Gifts and possessions of every kind are the fruit of effort: thoughts completed, goals reached, visions made real.
items.core_idea: Results match effort; there is no chance

items.plain: Calmness is a jewel of wisdom, earned by long patient self-control. As you understand yourself and others as shaped by thought, and see cause and effect more clearly, you stop fussing, worrying and grieving, and stay steady and serene.
items.core_idea: Understanding cause and effect brings calm

items.plain: Storm-tossed souls, the shore of your ideal awaits you. Hold the helm of thought firmly; the Master in your soul only sleeps, so wake Him. Self-control is strength, right thought mastery, calm power. Tell your heart: peace, be still.
items.core_idea: Steer by right thought; calm is power

items.plain: You, God, stir us to delight in praising You, because You made us for Yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.
items.core_idea: Our hearts are restless until they rest in God

items.plain: If only I could rest in You, God! If only You would enter my heart and fill it so I forget my troubles and embrace You, my only good!
items.core_idea: Longing for God to fill the heart

items.plain: My soul is a cramped house, God; enlarge it so You can enter. It is in ruins; repair it. It holds things that offend You, I admit. Who but You can cleanse it, and to whom else can I cry?
items.core_idea: Asking God to enlarge and cleanse the soul

items.plain: When adults idle it's called business; when boys do the same, those adults punish them, and no one pities either boys or men.
items.core_idea: Adults call their own idleness business

items.plain: You, God, have ordered it, and so it is: every disordered desire is its own punishment.
items.core_idea: Every disordered desire punishes itself

items.plain: My God, my true life, what does it matter that my speech was applauded above so many my own age? Isn't all of that just smoke and wind?
items.core_idea: Applause and praise are smoke and wind

items.plain: No one leaves You, God, or returns to You by travelling; the prodigal son needed no horses or ships to squander Your gifts far away. The true distance from Your face lies in lustful, darkened desires.
items.core_idea: Distance from God is in the heart, not in place

items.plain: A man seeking fame for eloquence, attacking his enemy with fierce hatred before a judge and crowd, watches carefully not to mispronounce the word "human being", but takes no care that his fury might destroy a real human being.
items.core_idea: We guard our words more than our victims

items.plain: My sin was looking for pleasure, greatness and truth not in God but in His creatures, myself and others, and so I fell headlong into sorrow, confusion and error.
items.core_idea: Seeking fulfilment in creatures, not God, leads to sorrow

items.plain: I recall my past corruption not because I love it but to love You, my God, that You may grow sweet to me and gather me up; turned from You, the One Good, I was lost among many things.
items.core_idea: Turned from God, the self scatters among many things

items.plain: All I wanted was to love and be loved, but I didn't keep to the bright limit of friendship between minds. Bodily desire and youthful urges clouded my heart until I couldn't tell clear love from the fog of lust.
items.core_idea: Desire can cloud the difference between love and lust

items.plain: You were always mercifully strict with me, Lord, mixing bitterness into my forbidden pleasures so I would seek pure pleasure, found only in You, who teach through sorrow, wound to heal, and kill lest we die apart from You.
items.core_idea: God wounds in order to heal

items.plain: Only vice deserves blame, yet I made myself out to be worse than I was to avoid blame, even claiming sins I hadn't committed so I wouldn't look contemptible for being innocent or less of a man for being chaste.
items.core_idea: Pretending to be worse to fit in with peers

items.plain: Each vice imitates You, God, badly: greed wants many things, but You own all; envy wants to excel, but who excels You; anger wants revenge, but You avenge most justly; fear wants safety, found only in You.
items.core_idea: Every vice is a distorted reach for what God has

items.plain: Who, knowing his own weakness, dares credit his purity and innocence to his own strength, loving You less as if he needed less of the mercy by which You forgive those who turn to You?
items.core_idea: No one is pure by their own strength

items.plain: O friendship too unfriendly! A baffling seducer of the soul, a hunger to do harm for fun, wanting others' loss with no gain for myself. When someone says "Let's go, let's do it," we're ashamed not to be shameless.
items.core_idea: In a group, we are ashamed not to be shameless

items.plain: I long for You, Righteousness and Innocence, beautiful and endlessly satisfying. In You is complete rest and untroubled life, free of fear. But in my youth I wandered far from You, my God, and became a barren land to myself.
items.core_idea: Wandering from God left me a barren land

items.plain: In Carthage unholy loves seethed around me. I wasn't yet in love, but loved the idea of loving and, from deep need, hated myself for not needing more. In love with love, I sought something to love, and hated safety.
items.core_idea: In love with love, searching for something to love

items.plain: In my studies I found Cicero's Hortensius, a call to philosophy. It changed my desires and turned my prayers to You, Lord; every empty hope became worthless, and I burned for immortal wisdom and began to return to You.
items.core_idea: One book can turn a life toward wisdom and God

items.plain: But You, God, were deeper within me than my deepest self, and higher than my highest.
items.core_idea: God is closer than our inmost self

items.plain: Through humble devotion we return to You, God: You cleanse our bad habits, pity those who confess, and free us from chains we made ourselves, unless we defy You with a false freedom, loving our private good above You.
items.core_idea: Humble return to God frees us from self-made chains

items.plain: Many acts people condemn, You, God, approve, and many they praise, You condemn, because the outward act, the doer's intention and the hidden needs of the moment all differ.
items.core_idea: God judges intention, not just outward acts

items.plain: You reached down, God, and drew my soul out of deep darkness, while my mother, Your faithful one, wept for me more than mothers weep over a child's death. She saw my spiritual death, and You heard her tears.
items.core_idea: A mother's tearful prayers are heard by God

items.plain: O good and all-powerful God, You care for each one of us as if we were the only one, and for all of us as if we were just one.
items.core_idea: God cares for each as if the only one

items.plain: Without You, God, what am I to myself but a guide to my own ruin? At best, what am I but an infant feeding on You, the food that never perishes? And what is any man, being only a man?
items.core_idea: Without God we only lead ourselves to ruin

items.plain: Grief darkened my heart; everything I saw was death. Home tormented me, and all I'd shared with my friend became torture without him. I searched everywhere and hated every place for lacking him. I became a riddle to myself.
items.core_idea: Grief turns every familiar place into torment

items.plain: You, God, remain in Yourself while we are tossed among trials; yet unless we could mourn to You, we would have no hope. How does sweetness come from groans, tears and complaints? Is it the hope that You hear us?
items.core_idea: Hope that God hears us sweetens our tears

items.plain: I was miserable, as is every soul bound in love to perishable things: losing them tears it apart, and it feels the misery it already had before. So I wept bitterly and found my only rest in bitterness.
items.core_idea: Clinging to perishable things makes loss tear us apart

items.plain: I marvelled that others lived on when he, whom I loved as if he'd never die, was dead, and more that I, his second self, lived. We were one soul in two bodies, and I couldn't bear living as half.
items.core_idea: Losing a dear friend feels like losing half your soul

items.plain: What madness, not knowing how to love humans as mortal! I chafed at the human lot, fretting and weeping, carrying a shattered, bleeding soul, and found nowhere to lay it down: not in groves, music, feasts, love-making or books.
items.core_idea: Grief finds no rest in any pleasure

items.plain: Where could my heart run from my heart? Where could I escape myself? Where would I not follow myself?
items.core_idea: You cannot run away from yourself

items.plain: Time never stands idle; through the senses it works strangely on the mind. Day by day it brought new images and memories and little by little patched me up with my old pleasures, and my sorrow gave way to them.
items.core_idea: Time slowly patches up grief

items.plain: Blessed is the one who loves You, God, and loves his friend in You and his enemy for Your sake. Only he loses no one dear, because all are dear to him in the One who cannot be lost.
items.core_idea: Love others in God, and none are truly lost

items.plain: Turn us, God of Hosts, show us Your face, and we will be whole. Wherever the human soul turns, except toward You, it gets fixed on sorrows, even when it is fixed on beautiful things.
items.core_idea: Apart from God, even beauty leads to sorrow

items.plain: Don't be foolish, my soul, or let the noise of your folly deafen your heart. Listen: the Word itself calls you to return, to a place of unshakable rest where love is not abandoned unless it abandons itself.
items.core_idea: The Word calls the soul back to lasting rest

items.plain: There is no rest where you are looking. Keep seeking what you seek, but it isn't where you are seeking it. You look for a blessed life in the land of death; it is not there.
items.core_idea: Lasting happiness isn't found where we usually look

items.plain: A human being is a great depth, Lord. You number even the hairs of his head and none falls without You, yet his hairs are easier to count than his feelings and the movements of his heart.
items.core_idea: The human heart is deeper than we can fathom

items.plain: Look how the weak soul lies flat when truth's solid ground doesn't hold it up! Blown by the gusts of opinionated people's words, it is pushed this way and that, its light clouded and the truth hidden from it.
items.core_idea: Without truth, the soul is blown about by opinions

items.plain: Lord, under the shadow of Your wings let us hope; carry us from childhood to old age. Our strength is real only when it is Yours. Let us return to You, our good; our home has not fallen.
items.core_idea: Our strength is God's; our home in Him stands

items.plain: All Your creation, God, never stops praising You, so that our weary souls may rise toward You, leaning on the things You made and passing on to You, their wonderful Maker; there we find refreshment and true strength.
items.core_idea: Creation lifts the weary soul toward God

items.plain: Where was I while I was looking for You, God? You were right before me, but I had gone away from You; I couldn't even find myself, let alone You.
items.core_idea: Lost to God, we are lost to ourselves

items.plain: You are great, Lord, and regard the humble, but see the proud from far away. You draw near only to the contrite, and the proud do not find You, even if they could count the stars and chart the planets.
items.core_idea: God is found by the humble, not the clever proud

items.plain: Does knowing all these things please You, God? Unhappy is the one who knows them all but not You; happy the one who knows You though not them. Knowing both makes one happier only because of You.
items.core_idea: Knowing God matters more than knowing everything else
